case_study_insert.main_stem: Harvestvale Dairy Co-operative (HDC) is a cooperative in the dairy farming and milk processing sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2004 by farmer Elena Harvestvale, it supplies yoghurt and cheese to independent grocers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. HDC plans to invest $960,000 in a new automated yoghurt and cheese processing plant, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 of member share capital. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. HDC faces two problems: milk spoilage waste has reached 4.1% and staff absenteeism is rising across the processing floor.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q4 2025: A survey of 750 shoppers at independent grocers found 72% would pay up to $0.80 more for locally sourced yoghurt and 61% read dairy-origin labels. In-store trials sold 31,000 pots with a complaint rate of 1.6%, down from 2.9% in the previous trial. Milk spoilage waste measured 4.1% of intake. Average delivery time to grocers is 2.7 days. Training logs show 22 of 64 staff have not finished on-the-job training on the new pasteurisers; off-the-job training at the agricultural college costs $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harvestvale Dairy Co-operative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.20 to $14.15 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Animal-feed and dairy input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 7.1%, while consumer spending on branded yoghurt grew 4.0% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HDC plans to fund part of its processing plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HDC of using member share capital instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Member share capital does not require the regular interest payments or capital repayments that a $560,000 bank loan demands, which protects the cooperative's cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year. The $400,000 raised from members can therefore be spent on the $960,000 processing plant rather than on servicing debt, and it helps absorb the 11.3% rise in animal-feed and dairy input costs without raising the $16.00 selling price for independent grocers.

Point 2: Share capital from members carries no collateral or repossession risk, so the new yoghurt and cheese plant cannot be seized if sales to grocers disappoint. It also preserves the cooperative's member ownership and democratic control, since no outside lender can impose conditions on how Elena Harvestvale and the members run the business. Because member shares are a permanent source of funds, HDC avoids the variable-rate exposure created when the base rate rose from 4.00% to 4.75%. Overall, member share capital lowers both the financing cost and the risk of the expansion compared with borrowing more from a bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HDC and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HDC is launching its new locally sourced yoghurt range. Consider a television advertising campaign, in-store tastings at grocers, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HDC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising campaign: Television would create fast, broad awareness of the new yoghurt range across many regions at once. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 64-member cooperative already funding a $960,000 plant with a $560,000 loan, and much of the audience will not shop at the independent grocers that stock HDC's cheese and yoghurt, so a significant part of the budget would be wasted.

In-store tastings at grocers: Tastings put the product directly in front of the shoppers who actually buy from independent grocers, let customers judge the taste of the locally sourced yoghurt, and can be tied to the 61% who read dairy-origin labels. The cost is modest and the feedback is immediate, but the reach is limited to stores already stocking HDC, so it cannot quickly build awareness across new outlets.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can tell the local-sourcing story to a wide audience at a low cost per reached shopper, and can point to the 72% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.80 more for locally sourced yoghurt. Results build slowly and depend on influencer credibility, and the audience is less certain to visit an independent grocer.

Recommendation: HDC should choose in-store tastings as the lead channel, with light social media support. Tastings convert the exact shoppers at the point of sale, suit a cooperative with $320,000 fixed costs, and directly demonstrate the local-sourcing benefit that the research values. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 64-employee cooperative, while influencer marketing is rejected as the main channel because its audience is diffuse and HDC's sales depend on independent grocers rather than national brand recognition.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HDC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HDC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and influencer marketing are rejected.

questions.question_text: HDC's milk spoilage waste has reached 4.1% and staff absenteeism is rising. Explain two benefits for HDC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation on the processing floor.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 64 employees a genuine voice in how the new yoghurt and cheese plant is organised, which satisfies social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set pasteuriser routines and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly tackling HDC's rising absenteeism and making the most of its flat structure.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions draws on the practical knowledge of the workers who handle milk every day, generating ideas that can reduce the 4.1% milk spoilage waste. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $950 per employee cost of off-the-job training at the agricultural college and protecting output of 110,000 units while the $960,000 plant beds in. Because the cooperative's members are also its workers, democratic decision-making strengthens their sense of ownership in Elena Harvestvale's business.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HDC's absenteeism, waste and output.

questions.question_text: HDC must upskill 22 processing staff to operate the new pasteurisers. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the agricultural college. Which should HDC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training 22 staff on HDC's own pasteurisers is directly relevant to the cooperative's exact settings and hygiene standards, costs nothing in external fees, and keeps those workers productive while they learn, protecting output toward 110,000 units and the drive to cut the 4.1% spoilage waste. The drawback is that the trainers are themselves processing staff whose own work suffers, and bad habits can be passed on, which matters when complaint rates are being monitored.

Off-the-job training: The agricultural college course at $950 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 staff, costing $20,900 in total — modest beside the $960,000 plant. It removes 22 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity and risking more spoilage, and the generic content may not match HDC's exact pasteuriser settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed.

Decision: HDC should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short college sessions later for the most senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, equipment-specific and avoids losing capacity while spoilage and absenteeism are already concerns; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $20,900 and 22 staff from a new plant would jeopardise supply to independent grocers, and the cooperative can add college certification once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HDC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HDC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HDC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $320,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $8.00) = $320,000 ÷ $8.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $8.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HDC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HDC's managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 110,000 units to confirm the new plant is comfortably profitable, giving a margin of safety of 70,000 units, which supports running the $960,000 facility at full capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets HDC model the $0.80 premium for locally sourced yoghurt: if won, contribution rises toward $8.80, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $320,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $320,000 and contribution of $8.00 lets managers set the sales volume needed to service the $560,000 bank loan and check the plant can afford the repayments before committing more member capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost ($320,000 ÷ 110,000 units + $8.00 = $10.91 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, isolate the 4.1% milk spoilage waste, and judge whether to renegotiate the $8.00 variable cost given 11.3% dairy input inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 110,000-unit output; the $0.80 local-sourcing premium against $320,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $560,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.91 to tackle 4.1% spoilage.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HDC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HDC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.75 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $110,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $300,000; 2025 current assets = $130,000 + $140,000 + $80,000 = $350,000. Liquidity cover for 2024 = $300,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.50, and for 2025 = $350,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.75. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($300,000 − $150,000) ÷ $200,000 = $150,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.75, and 2025 = ($350,000 − $130,000) ÷ $200,000 = $220,000 ÷ $200,000 = 1.10.

Evaluation: HDC's short-term liquidity has strengthened clearly. The first ratio rose from 1.50 to 1.75 as current assets grew from $300,000 to $350,000 while current liabilities stayed at $200,000, so the cooperative covers its short-term obligations more comfortably. The second ratio, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.75 to 1.10, meaning HDC no longer depends on selling yogurt and cheese stock to meet debts — valuable while it services a $560,000 bank loan and builds a $960,000 plant. However, trade receivables rose from $110,000 to $140,000, tying up cash; if independent grocers pay late the improvement could unwind, and the fall in inventories to $130,000 should be watched to avoid shortages.

Conclusion: HDC's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.50 to 1.75 and 0.75 to 1.10) and the gain does not rely on stock. The main residual risk is higher receivables, so HDC should tighten credit control with grocers while proceeding with the processing investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HDC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HDC of promoting its yoghurt as locally sourced.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Promoting the yoghurt as locally sourced matches the 72% of 750 surveyed shoppers who would pay up to $0.80 more for locally sourced yoghurt, letting HDC charge a premium that protects the $8.00 contribution per unit even as dairy input costs rise 11.3%. It also appeals to the 61% who read dairy-origin labels, strengthening loyalty among shoppers at independent grocers and supporting sales from the $960,000 plant.

Disadvantage: A local-sourcing claim can limit HDC's ability to buy cheaper milk from other regions, keeping the $8.00 variable cost per unit higher than a national competitor's. It also depends on a steady local milk supply: a poor harvest or herd disease could raise costs or interrupt production, and the 4.1% spoilage waste would make any premium harder to deliver consistently.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HDC's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in input costs will affect HDC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If HDC's $560,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $560,000 = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × $560,000). That is modest against $320,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $960,000 plant, but HDC can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $14.15 an hour): HDC employs a workforce of 64 in processing and packing, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 64 staff = 1,718.75 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $8.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (11.3% animal feed and dairy): HDC's $8.00 variable cost per unit contains milk and feed inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3% that adds about 11.3% × $8.00 = $0.90 per unit, and at 110,000 units that is roughly $99,000 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.80 local-sourcing premium and grocer price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 110,000 units and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution that justifies the $960,000 plant, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $4,200, so both are smaller.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HDC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HDC with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
